title: Joseph Rene and Edna Kelly Interview, 1969-12-15

blocks.x: What's up with Michael? What do you think of your... You know, I mean, I'm sorry to entice him. They get a plan there. Yeah. Because you see he was playing. He was playing flute one day. One of them little fights. That's right, yes. And I passed that and I hold that and I stopped looking. I said, Oh, this fella can play on some fight. So, I went to talk with him. I asked him, I said, Well, I think you can make a good planet player.
Yes.

Think you can make a good planet player. So what I did, I talked him up and I let him play a couple of pieces. I said, well, how do you make your sharks and how do you make your flat? They ain't nothing but natural. No, they ain't but six holes. You see. He told me when I want to make a shark like that, he said, I want to make a shark like that. He said, I lose the top of the hole and I blow hard. And when I want to make a flat, he said, I just cover half of the hole. So, I called himself, I said, you know what I'm saying? I believe you could be a good planet player. I said, the way you play with them fights and what you could do to land on them six fingers, I said, now they got shark keys and everything, you know. Yeah. Because I used to play planet myself, you see. So, sure enough, I kept on talking with him and went up on a rap wall street and he got them playing that. And he stood around there and what he used to make on that flute, he used to make it on them six holes, you see. But he tried to make them same thing with them shelf and flat with that, but I told him, no. I showed him where the keys was. Where did you hear him playing flute when you thought he was like that? Governor Nicholson, between Murray, I can't remember the number that's on the song, Governor Nicholson, between Murray and Liberty.

But was this where he was living? That's where he was living at that time. Was he living there with his wife then or with his mother? Well, he had a wife, a common old wife. Yes, I know who you mean actually because her name is Emma. Emma. Emma Zeno. Emma Zeno. And I met her the other day and she remembered you actually. She remembered me. Yes, I was asking her about who she remembered of the musicians that George played with and you were about the only one she remembered.

Yeah, yeah. Well, he played a while with us. He played a while with us because it didn't take him no time. He used to practice by himself, you know. I tried to get him to learn how to read. He couldn't read no music.
No.

I tried to get him to learn how to read but it seemed like he could more at ease from here. Yes. And he turned out to be a real good, good class, good jazz class. Yes. And around the corner from there, there where Shield used to live. Remember the Dixieland band, the first Dixieland band? Yes.
Them five?
Yes, I know. Tin Roof. Yeah.
Well, they were living right around the corner. Around from Governor Nichols?
Yeah, right there, yeah, on the street between Governor Nichols and Barracks. There in the shop there used to. And that boy just came up on the planet just like that. Yeah.
And he got the planes, so everybody warned him, you know. Who were you talking about now, George? George Lewis, yeah. A lot of fellas warned him.

He went with different fellas and played music. He played with Sam Morgan, some. He played a few jobs with us, you know. And he played with Chris Kellys. Oh, yeah, that's about. Then he formed up his own band. Yeah. Formed off the board. George Lewis band. He got, first he had, oh no, he played with Kid Howard. Yes. Remember Kid Howard? Yes. Yeah, well, he played with him. But when he got out from Kid Howard, that way he formed his own band. He got this fella, Slowdrag, you know what you talking about? He played bass and he got this Jim Crow, what they call Jim Robinson. He played the trambone and he got there. And let's see who he got. He had another fella. Oh, Moreira on Band. Right. Lawrence. Lawrence. Lawrence.

And that's John Forkartin. Who was drumming with him? Well, he had, of course in the late years he had Joe Watkins. Who? Joe Watkins. Joe Watkins. Well, he was a much more recent drummer. You probably don't even remember him. Yeah, no. He died fairly recently.

Yeah, yeah. Well, there's another fella. I can't think of his name. He had a drummer. He tried to get me with him and I said, no, I wouldn't. I was going to leave my brother, you know. We had such, you know, good, wonderful band. I guess you must have heard.
I talked about it. Did you stay more or less continually playing with your brother all the time?
Yeah. Yeah. I continued. Then after we just couldn't get no work, things went bad, you know. Then we dissolved the band. That was when?
In the 30s?
Yeah, that's right. Let's see. No, that's when I'm 32. And then 35 I went out there. You know where we talk about the Budweiser?
Yeah, I heard of that.

I know where you, on Ivyville. Yeah, that's right. I played there five years. I played from, oh, I retired. I played from 35 up to 42. 35 up to 42 I played there with a fella that's called Rap. I don't know if you've already talked about him. Played guitar. Rap, yeah, that's right. And young, you call him Spook. And handy, played the bass. And Decaugé, you might have heard him talk about him. I would have been playing the write-up about him. Decaugé. No, I don't think I know.
No? That was a wonderful piano player.

Yeah. Decaugé, yeah. And did you have on there? Yeah. Eh? Decaugé, uh, well, we had, uh, when I went, they had, they got rid of this band. See, because a couple of the musicians quit the thing, and they got rid of them. So, the man told them, say, I know two fellas out in Gitts, I'm gonna see them. He said, that's, uh, Rainey, Kid Rainey and his brother, Joe Rainey. So they came and got us, man. We went up in there, man. Kept that house packed. We kept that house packed for them number of years. Then in 42, well, because they got killed. I mean, right above, they got killed. Stabbed. Well, them fellas, well, them fellas, uh, they didn't like the religion I had. They didn't like the religion. So, they said, if I catch you asleep, we're gonna find him. And so what they did, they got rid of me, see, because I would, you know, drink a long water, you see. This fella spoke young, I don't know if you know. Boy, that fella used to get drunk every night. Then he'd get off and go at the light and you could, around 10 o'clock, 11 o'clock in the daytime, you could find him around Ramport Street Stagg. And I don't understand. And he was a great musician. Anything you throw up there, he could play it right off just like that.
Very huge.
You know, another fella, too, I was, uh, you know, I was with him when he got first got to Sidney Bichet, you ever heard of him?
Oh, yeah. Yeah.
Well, I got, you know, you don't want, but Joe Lewis, because I'll tell you, not here. Well, that's all right.
That's all right.

Well, anyhow, I'll get back on Joe Lewis while he came to me. He got, Sidney, he was another fella who played that little fight. He, another fella, could play a fight. So, we, I'll tell you how we had, we had a little band. I went and got some skin off a round steak and dried it and made a drum. My brother had a corn and a piece of silver pig on it. And he would play there like a trumpet. And Bichet, he had the flute. And another fella, well, he turned out to be a garbage court driver. He turned out to be a little garbage wagon. He was the only fella that didn't come out to be a musician. I come out to be a drummer, my brother came to be a trumpet. And Bichet got a clanded. But we spread off then. This is when you first started, in other words, you're talking about it. Oh, yeah. That's what you were talking about then.
Yeah, that's right. That's back at that time. When would that have been, do you think? Oh, yeah.
That's what you were talking about then. Oh, I was a kid then.
Oh, I see. Yeah, I was a kid.
I would put myself about this age, and Bichet went to school together. I put my age about around twelve to thirteen years old at that time.

Bichet was, I'm trying to think, when he was born, he would have been a little bit older than he would have been, Sidney Bichet. Uh, I don't know. See, when were you born? What was the, uh... Me? I was born in 73. You were born in 1890? 1897. 1897, yes. Yeah, born in 1893. And your brother? I forgot what he was born. But was he, he was, was he older than you or younger than me? No, he was younger than me. Oh, he was younger than me. Yeah. He was along with Lewis, you know. Oh, I see. Yeah, Lewis, I don't know. That's another color used to go out of bands sometime.

You know, the white folks used to have them picking, I don't know, no, I don't think you're old enough to remember Millenburg, Camps. Hey, you're parked! No, I didn't remember Millenburg. Millenburg, West End, they used to have camps. And just about from here to that kitchen, that's just how for a camp, then. And boy, you're talking about, they used to have a Spanish fort, uh, stuff to that kitchen. That is how far the camp's been. And boy, you're talking about, you used to have a Spanish fourth call run out there. It had about two, three cars hooked onto it, you know. And boy, you're talking about bass drums and basses. All the things that be loaded. One camp, fellas blowing that one another. You remember a fella too, Blind Gilbert, you ever heard of him? Who? Blind Gilbert. Gilby, no. White fella. Blind. No, I don't think I did. I had right up with him because he played plenty of trumpets. Oh yeah, Gilbert played up some trumpets. Gilbert. You know what band we used to work close with? You know, Sharky. Yes, I heard that. I knew Sharky is
a good friend of your brother's. Yeah, that's right. We used to play all the jobs that he couldn't take.
He'd give it to us. That's how we worked together. He's still playing it, I think. Oh, sure. Yeah.
Nice trumpet. Did he play somewhat similar to your brother? Didn't he sort of copy your brother?

Yeah. Yeah. And you know who played? He played like my brother played trumpet. P-Fa. That's the way my brother played trumpet. Just like that. Play it like that. You ever notice he plays? He makes his rung and thing, but he never gets away from his melody. Never get away from it. It stays right there with the melody.
Yeah. Now you pronounce your name Rene, don't you? Rene Everson. Your brother, you spell it R-E-N-A. Well, now, you see, we used to spell it R-E-N-A. Yes.

But one time come, I had to have my voice that people would find it was R-E-N-E. Instead of Rene, instead of E, instead of A, it's E. See, you know how Creole people, always used things backwards. Now that, he had the sound of E, you see, and we used to go by that.

But it was R-E-N-E. That was quite serious. How did your brother pronounce it? Did you pronounce it Rene the same? Yeah, that's all right. Now, how did you actually, can you remember how you actually first met George when you were saying, like up there on Governor Nicholson? On Governor Nicholson? Yeah, I mean, I was passing. Remember, I tell you that, I was passing.

And I heard a flute playing, and I was wondering who, he was living in the back. See, right section, the other half of the house. And I stand up, I stand, I must have stand up there about 15 minutes, listen to that cover. I said, I'm going to go talk to this fellow. I didn't even know his name. I said, man, when he come in, oh, God, I said,
Mr. Rene, he said, oh yeah, come on in, Rene.

I got to talk, and I said, oh, you playing that flute? I said, you play that flute? Well, good. Then I began questioning him about making them shorts and them flats, you see. Right. Because the fellow didn't know how to make them kind of things on the flute can't do nothing, but he did, you see. Then he could blow his soul powerful, then he could force some different tones out of it. The boy could hear him play a fight. Him and Bé-Shane played the same way. I said, I told him, I said, look, I said, I think we might need a clan that's here. I said, I think you could make a good clan that's here. So, sure enough, went and found Ramport Street. And before I know he hadn't bought the clan there,
he went and bought the clan there. He got a beef-like clan there. Can you remember the name of where he bought it? Oh, let's see. You know, you weren't talking about it.

of Fink, it's the Eagle Loan office, not... It's the what? Eagle Loan office. Yes. His wife, but I think his wife doesn't matter. You see old man Fink, and that's who's his son's wife. She's there now, deals with her right now. And I think that's where he bought that plan, because mostly everybody, most all cut cutters, who they deal with Fink. He doesn't deal with nobody else. And most of his deal, just with Fink, he was living... He was on Ramport, he was driving and he was dealing. Right across the street from
that store where we played that number, yes. Oh, I see. That's right downtown. Huh?
That's right downtown. Yeah, see. Then after the name of the old lady, the Tick Tock.

I think that broke that building down, didn't it? Did you get... Did you go back off and then... Did you become friends of George? Did you probably become a friend of the family or something? Because I was wondering how it was that his wife, Emma, Emma Zeno, George's name was Zeno, you know, really. When you first ran... Yeah, yeah, Zeno. Yeah, I knew that... He didn't change... But listen, that... That wouldn't be right. Well, they weren't married, but they were living together. Yeah, they were living together. And they... Did she start from the door? Yeah, that was...
Oh, that's all them children... They had about four boys, yeah. Yeah, that's right. Four boys and a couple of girls. Yeah, that's the same one, eh? Yeah.

She's still alive. She's up there, still up there on... Right in the same district by St. Thornton, eh? And there she's lying in the government, because I was up there. See, I've been up in that same shape, man. Yeah.
Oh, if you ever... You got my phone number, man. Yeah. Well, I want you to call me. You ever found out where I ever talk with her?

Well, yeah, I'll give you... I think I can probably give you her phone number, because I think I saw Habit somewhere. But I'll write it down for you. Okay. I'll probably have it here. I used to. I sure want to... But you see, she remembered you, and I asked her...

Yeah, I can tell you... I was asking about the musicians that you all played with, and she said, oh, it was Joe Rene. I remember him. Yeah, because I used to go in his house all the time. After he got that plan, I'd just... I would stick with him, you know? Still want to see her. I haven't seen her in a long time. I've got 15, 20 years almost.

Let's see. 525... 6093. It's 1204 Echelon. She lives there with her daughter, Mildred. Mildred. Oh, yeah. And she could probably have been a baby almost when you... that first time you were talking about when you went around and you heard your daughter playing the fight. Mildred, I want Mildred, but... Mildred was born in 1919. George would have been 19 years old when she was born. Actually, George was probably a little bit... I think she was a baby then. Yeah, or may not have even been born even. Maybe even... Yeah, that's right. Because the time you're talking about, George may have been only about 17 or 18. Quite young, I think. Yeah, yeah, yeah. Yeah, he... Tell me some of the places where you played with George when he played with you and your brother and so on.

Well, we used to play dances. We played dances. If I can remember that. You got something... I got to dig my mind now. Because he just... he didn't regularly say he played with the band. Studies. We used to iron. Yeah. We used to iron, yeah. Let's see if I had something to think about now. Well, we used to play that. Oh, I know he never played at the colony. He'd incorporate all over with us. Because we had a fella. Zeb DeMorris played at the colony at that time.
Was he more your regular kind of player?

Yeah, who? Zeb. Zeb, yeah. He was our regular kind of player. Oh, I know. I know. He used to play... I've never seen him ever play... He used to play cland on the side like that. Really? Yeah. He played a cland on the... Oh, it! Yeah, the style is odd. That's right. He had a cland in there. He had a cland in there. He had a cland in there.
I don't understand. What was he... Was he any good?

Oh, he had a cland in style, but I didn't like it. I didn't like his style. He had some kind of variation he made there. But it looked like to me, it was a little cland off, you know. He didn't have the real homie, you know. See, like George, like George said, but he stood right in homie, right in the key, you know. But all that stuff he made, he stood right there in the key. But once he looked like he was kind of... I never did like it. I used to come up with all the time. I said, okay. I tried to get a real good cland in there.
Did you ever hear Johnny Dodds play?

Yeah, sure. Sure, he used to play with Ori. I was a kid then. Johnny Dodds, he used to play at the Columny Hall. Johnny Dodds and his baby... Baby Dodds was his brother. He played drum with Ori. Kid Ori's band. I remember that. I used to come around and listen to some fellas, you know.
That must have been a pretty good band, I should think, wasn't it?
Oh yeah, yeah. Kid Ori had a nice band.
What do you think about... Who do you think of the best cland in the players you remember hearing in New Orleans?
Best cland in the players? Sidney Basia. He was tough. Nobody could beat that fella playing playing. He could take cland in and take it and happen.
I'll tell you something. You know something? You look a bit like Sidney Basia. Best cland in the pictures I see. The same song. Yeah, yeah.

I used to go to school with him and I used to beat him every day and take his lunch. Where about did you go to school? It was a private school. Miss Stephon. Not Miss Stephon. Miss Atkins. That school was on, uh, let's see, on Calarit. Yes. It was on Calarit between one or two schools. Calarit between Burgundy and Dauphin.
Oh yeah. That's close. George went to a private school. He said, Professor Medard Nelson, do you remember his name? Medard. Medard Nelson.
I would talk of him, but I forgot even what the school was. Medard.
That was somewhere on Burgundy, I think. Oh yeah. By a mother for Cabrini's.
Yeah, yeah, yeah. Oh boy, that was a stiff teacher. That's what I heard, yeah. He was stiff. He was stiff. Yeah, you had to learn there. Yeah. You had to learn. Never wanted to go to school there.

Did you ever meet George's mother? George's mother? No, I don't believe I met George's mother. I don't believe I ever met her. I can't remember meeting her. She's an older lady. She's, she died only a few years ago. She was about nearly a hundred, I think she's.

Yeah. I might have been George with the rifle. We supposed to get it plenty, you know. And George, I can't remember, I can't even tell you that, but I seen his mother in life. I might have though. I might have went to his mother, but I can't remember. You see. But I know his wife good, see. I used to be there all the time. I used to go on Rapport Street to get that red bean and them ham skin. He used to love red beans. And I'd come back and cook red beans and grab that horn. Soon he'd get through. Yeah, I bet he was a good cook, you know. How did he experience it? Oh yeah. Well, he could, he could, I don't care who didn't like beans, he'd make you eat beans. He'd get that ham skin. They don't sell that no more now. He's got that ham skin. You see, they take it off the bacon. And they'd roll that up and sell that for ten cents. Oh, you're talking about seasoned beans. That's sure the seasoned beans were. John Lewis was alright little fellow so much. He was like two men and women, so. Boy. Was he always like that? Eh? Was he always like that? From the time I knew it. From the time I knew it.
We're putting together sand in it. We took off, but you know, it's the bubbly area, you know. Yeah. Yeah. We're up to prosper. But he always was skinny.
And he used to eat, a guy could eat a pan of beans and rice, but he never get fat. Never stuff
I heard that. When I was there, I happened to pick up a paper.
Father told me, you're a musician across the river. Father named George. I said, what do you play?
I don't know what he played, but I know he's called George.

Or George Lewis. He used to go by the name of Lewis, but his right name was Zeno, like he said. Yeah. I don't know how he got that Lewis paper mixed up in there. And he got all his shirt under that same name. He got all his what? All his children under the same name, Lewis. All his what? Sorry. All his children.
Children, yeah. Yes, I think they are Lewis too.
Yeah, they're all Lewis.
Yes.
I don't know why he wouldn't pick that name, Zeno.
Yeah. They just started to call him that, I think, and he just decided to change his name because everybody was calling him George Lewis.
Yeah, just like one of our names was Ariane. Well, Ariane, you see. Well, after I got things straight, then I said, well, I just let it stay like that.
But after I got from this Christian organization, then I had to have everything correct, you see. Yeah. Yeah.

So I went down to the Catholic Church. I was born to the Catholic Church. I went down there, and I got my boy's sister, and I was surprised. And I always owned the impression that I was born with Marshall Levin, or the first. But when I look on that verse, it was Marshall Levin. Marshall Levin. Mm. Marshall Levin, 1897. My dad was a musician too. Oh, was he? Yeah. He used to play guitar, bandolin, bass. What was his name? Henry, Renny. He was working for a lot of war lines when they was on Burgundy Street. That's up I remember. That's your, I was a child then. And I understand, from what I can understand from old him, he's the first fella that thought to puttin' that twirl in the guitar. I mean? But when he wanted to play guitar, it's a different position. He didn't know how to make it. I couldn't remember, so he put it down in the market with some buttons off his shirt. That's, that's facts. I was surprised when a fella told that. Yeah. Do you remember Buddy Petit? Oh yeah, sure. I played with Buddy Petit. What did you think of him, Mr. Trumpet, right? Boy, he, he had a nice start. He's the first one to start with them derbies, you know, put them derbies on there. And, the way it is at that time, trumpet players ain't that way now, I don't agree. But, the other trumpet always tried to do one another. See? So, when I seen him at the derby, derby, derby, derby, I went out to the fresh market and got a coconut. Cut it in half. And, they ain't no brother do this, I don't want to trumpet, wah-wah. That's where they, that wah-wah started.
Mm-hmm.
Wah-wah, we started from there. Mm-hmm. Yeah. That's right. I'll never forget that.
How about Chris Kelly?

No, he started out there in the country down the, like the fella said, down the bayou, yeah. So, he was mostly of a blues player. He was, he was, like this, what you call it, I would call it at that time, not a, a blues player, that's all we would say. Yes, yes. He could play blues, you know, he could play that. He played other things, but he wouldn't have had a nice tone in his trumpet. My brother had the best tone in the world. Yeah. According to what this, uh, this, uh, French professor in France said, you know. Oh, yeah. And, they, they went and viewed him some of them, and, and he was talking about the colored trumpet players. And, they, they all of them. And, they said, my brother had the best tone, the best tone trumpet. Oh, yeah.
Oh, yeah.

Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. And, you see, his jaws was flattened. You see no jaws popping like that. Played this as smooth. He wasn't excited about nothing. Mm-hmm. At that time, we had, they used to call, you ever heard of him talking about the tailgate? We used to be advertising, and, well, at one place we started in the furniture way. Two mules. Then, after that, there came, uh, these trucks. And, the trombone player, and the bass player, the one, beat all the tailgates. All the rest of the music. Yeah. Yeah. There used to be a time, man. We used to meet them bands, meet on the corner, man. And, they tied them trucks together. All the people, you know, people outside did that. They know he's gonna beat them bands. They know he's gonna beat them bands. They know he's gonna beat them bands.
They would let them go away, because when they see us coming, they get out of the way.
You made a recording, didn't you, with your brother?
Yeah, that's right.
I thought it was kind of difficult to get those records.

I don't know if you can go to Ikes for King René's Delta Giant Band. The Giant Band, you can get it under that name. They got the history and everything. I don't know the record to a fella. I had it here for quite a while. And a fella wanted so bad, so I don't know if I can take it. I ain't gonna use it, just let somebody get it. Sure. You know Dick Allen? Yeah, sure. I bet you can get that record from him.
Oh yeah, he's got copies of them up at the Tulane Library.
Yeah, that's right. That's why I went up there and got that record.
Yeah.
Yeah.
He told me, I forgot all about it. Yeah, it was him who gave me your... And Buck Johnson on the other side. That's right. I know the record.
Yeah, Buck Johnson on the other side.

Yeah, the fella that made those records, Hayward Broon, you know, Woody Broon, I guess is David. You see him on television sometimes. No, no. You ever seen him? No, no, no. He does a sports thing for CBS. You may not. I don't know if you watch it. He always wears striped blazers and everything. Handled by a mustache. Yeah. I might...
He's the same guy. Yeah, what Charlie come on? Four. Charlie Four? Charlie Four?
Mm-hmm.
Yeah, what...
You sometimes see him on sports. He always does things on sports. Oh, on sports, eh?
Yeah.
Oh, yeah.
On national television, not local. Oh, not local. National. National.
But, uh... That's the guy who he was. Yeah. Well, it looks like...
They had another clan player who used to play with us. I don't get no record of him. And he does play a wonderful clan in him. They call him, uh, Freddie Small. I met him the other day. Yeah?
Blind fellow.
He can give you plenty of history, so I could find these out.
Freddie Small?
Huh? Freddie Small. Yeah. He's a blind fellow. Some kind of preacher, huh? Boy, he could tell you something. He told me some things about myself I didn't know.
Really?
That's right. He's a good memory. Oh, yeah. He's good on that. Very good memory. Yeah, I never was.
Yeah, he played with us, too. Yeah, he's smaller. He passes every day, him and his wife. He's a kind of player. Used to be. And play harmonica.
Used to be harmonica, too. I don't know if he would still play harmonica. But he's...
He was a very good clan that's for me.

You know, he reminds me, he used to be stuff Oh yeah, he's right up in my age, maybe a little younger. Can't be too much. Can't be too much older and can't be too much younger. Yeah. I'm gonna, give me your hand here for something. I'm gonna let you get attention to that fella, that fella could tell you some things, but a very good memory, his phone number.

We're interviewing, see if we're getting a... Yeah, that's alright. We're interviewing Edna Kelly and today is December 15th, 1969. And let's see, it's 1907, the Feet Street, which you think. Alright, well, you're one of the few people, of course, that are alive now that would know anything, if you'd be able to tell us anything about Chris Kelly. And can you tell me when you were born? What was, what, what year were you born in? 1911. Pardon? 1911. 1911. I'm 50.
Got me off for the love. I'm 62, I'm 61 years old. I'm 61, so that would be 60. Ah, 1908 I guess.
1908, that's right.
And Chris was, was he a good deal older than you? Do you remember, do you know what year he was born?
Well, I don't know, cause you see, he was much older man than I was. I was a young girl at the time.
Yes. He must have been, I don't know when he was born. He must have been in his age, but anyway, I liked him.
Yes. And you don't know how old he was when you married him? Well, he said he was 29, but I know he wasn't. He told my mother that. You see, I got...
Yes. What year were you married him? Do you remember what year you were married? I can't remember. No. Well, um... But you were quite young when you married him.
Quite young. Yes. As soon as he, my son born, when I was 16. Oh really? I was with my son born. Yes. And I was going with him about, say about a year before then. Yeah.
I see. Um... Where, where, when you, where did you live with, with Chris?
We lived on Robinson between Conte and Bienville. Yes. 326 North Robinson Street. Then we moved from there and we lived on Villery Street. Right around the corner. I see.
And, um, um, can you tell me something about, uh, what did Chris looked like?
